rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · The Learned Gentleman
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a poor scholar's room lit by a green-shaded lamp, an elderly Edwardian gentleman with spectacles reading aloud from a glowing half-moon amulet of red gold held by a tall Egyptian priest in spotted robes, bookshelves and papers everywhere, ink pots and dust in the lamplight, warm amber against deep shadow, mysterious gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: The children's lodgings belonged to old Nurse, and upstairs lived a learned gentleman who studied old Egypt. He knew its gods, its tombs, and its forgotten words, and he was poor as a church mouse. His room smelled of ink and dust, and the children thought him the wisest man in London. Every evening his lamp burned late, and every morning his eyes were kind behind his spectacles.
The learned gentleman reads the Amulet's writing, written three thousand years ago.

One evening they brought Rekh-ma-ra up the narrow stairs. The learned gentleman looked at the priest's bronze collar and strange robes. The Amulet hung between them, glowing very faintly, like a lamp turned low. Then he read aloud the writing on the Amulet, slowly, in the old tongue. The priest answered in the same. For one moment, the two men three thousand years apart talked together like old schoolfellows.
New word: scholar - someone who spends a whole life learning. The learned gentleman could read the Amulet's writing, though he never guessed where it came from.

"Your people built for ever," said the learned gentleman, wondering. "And mine endured," said Rekh-ma-ra, "by the mercy of the gods and the labor of the poor. Pray for both, brother." Then the Amulet's glow faded, and the priest stepped back into his own time. The room was only a poor man's room again. The learned gentleman looked after him for a long time.

The Psammead, sulking in its basket, opened one snail eye. "You are learning," it said grudgingly, "that time is full of people, and people are all alike." The children laughed. Outside, the London fog muffled the streets, and the house was quiet. But Anthea wrote in her secret book that night. She wrote: the Great Wish is coming near, and we must be ready to choose it well.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · The City of the Future
chapters.artPrompt: a future London of tall pale buildings with hanging gardens and quiet clean streets, flying machines gliding overhead like gentle birds, four Edwardian children in old-fashioned clothes standing amazed on a wide sunny pavement, a kind woman gesturing toward a marble hall, bright hopeful daylight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: "Show us the future," said Robert one evening, holding up the joined Amulet. The Psammead snorted, and the Amulet grew bright as a little moon. London melted away like sugar in warm water. The children stood in the same streets, and yet everything was changed. There were tall fair buildings, gardens on the roofs, and clean air. And there were no hungry faces anywhere.
The future London is fair and kind, like a city built by friends.

People moved slowly and laughed easily. Machines flew overhead like quiet birds, and the schools had open doors. There were no beggars, and no locked doors, and no children going hungry to school. A kind-faced woman showed them a marble hall and told them proudly, "This was once a slum. We are still mending what your age left us - but we are mending it."
Question for you: The future is not perfect, only better. Who does the Amulet suggest is building that better time, slowly, all the time?

"It is being built now," said the Psammead, reading the children's thoughts exactly. "By every one who is kind today. You saw it: the walls of your own days, seen from the far side." The children were quiet all the way home, the way one is quiet after music. Robert carried the memory of that marble hall for the rest of his life.

They came home to their own foggy, hurried London, and it seemed smaller and noisier than before. But it was theirs, and it was now. And now, the Psammead reminded them, is where every future is built. The fog rolled up round the lamps, and old Nurse had supper waiting. "Choose your Great Wish soon," it said. "The Amulet is ready, and so, my dears, must you be."

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · Choosing the Wish
chapters.artPrompt: four Edwardian children around a lamplit parlor table with small papers spread out, reading their wishes aloud to one another, a small brown furry creature with snail eyes on stalks sitting up on the armchair like a judge, the joined glowing amulet hanging from a nail on the wall, warm lamplight and deep shadows, tender storybook illustration

blocks.text: Now came the hardest part, and it was not magic at all. The whole Amulet, the Psammead explained, would grant the wish of their hearts - once. Only once, and then its work would be done. The Psammead sat up on the arm of the chair to listen, like a small brown judge. So each child wrote a wish on paper, and they read them out by lamplight.
By lamplight the children read out their wishes, and think of one another.

Cyril wished Father's ship safe from the stormy seas. Robert wished Mother well again in the far southern hospital. Anthea wished the Lamb home from the country, laughing. The papers trembled a little, for wishes written down look very bare. And Jane's paper said simply: "All of them. All of us. All together." Nobody laughed at Jane's wish. It was the best of the four.
Talk together: Each child wants something different, and every wish is good. How do you choose one wish for a whole family?

"Cannot we wish all four things?" asked Robert. "You may," said the Psammead, "if you can find the wish that holds all four inside it. A great wish is like a great coat. It must be cut wide enough for everybody." So they thought, and argued, and thought again, for three whole evenings. Jane cried a little at night, and nobody mentioned it in the morning.

At last Anthea wrote one sentence on a fresh paper, and they all put their hands over her hand. They did not say it aloud yet. A wish like theirs, they felt, should be spoken standing, in a ring. The Amulet should be hanging in the moonlight, and the hearts ready. Outside, the moon was rising over the chimney pots, large and calm.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Great Wish
chapters.artPrompt: four Edwardian children standing in a ring in a moonlit parlor, a joined moon-shaped amulet of red gold blazing like a small golden moon in a girl's outstretched hands, a small brown creature with snail eyes watching from an armchair, moonlight through tall windows and a hint of garden beyond, solemn magical storybook illustration

blocks.text: On a clear night, with the moon on the garden, the four children stood in a ring. The whole Amulet hung from Anthea's hands, glowing like a little golden moon. The Amulet was heavy, and heavier still with everything it held. The Psammead sat up on its haunches to watch. Together, in one voice, they spoke the wish they had chosen. "Let us be all together, and all safe, and let those we love be happy."
The joined Amulet blazes, and the Great Wish goes out into the world.

The Amulet flared till it filled the room with morning. Then it grew quiet, and warm, and ordinary - and nothing else happened at all. The children looked at one another. "Has it worked?" whispered Jane. "It is working," said the Psammead. "A wish of that size is not a match struck in the dark. It is a seed. It will grow in its own right time." The Psammead's fur stood up like bristles of a brush.
Question for you: The Great Wish does not come true in one second. Why is waiting, and helping, sometimes part of a wish?

"And what do we do now?" asked Robert. "What you always do," said the Psammead. "Write to Father. Be good to old Nurse. Take the learned gentleman his slippers. A wish is not a chair to sit in, child. It is a road to walk." Robert went up the stairs two at a time, to fetch the slippers.

So the days went on much as before, with school and errands and letters crossed out and rewritten. But now there was a secret gladness under everything, like a fire lit but banked. Somewhere on the sea, a ship was turning toward home. Somewhere in a hospital garden, the sun came out. And the moon went on rising, over everything, patient as a friend.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Good News
chapters.artPrompt: a cozy Edwardian parlor where four children dance and wave three opened letters, an old nurse in a print apron laughing with her hands to her face, envelopes with ship and flower seals on the table, a small brown creature with snail eyes watching from an armchair, warm firelight and lamplight, joyful storybook illustration

blocks.text: The good news came the way spring comes - in small signs, then all together. First a letter from the shipping line: Father's ship had come safe through the great storm, and was homeward bound. The envelope was fat, and the seal was a ship in full sail. Old Nurse read it three times and put her apron over her face.
One by one the good letters arrive, like spring after a long winter.

Then a letter from the south, in Mother's own hand. The doctors were pleased, it said. She could sit in the garden now. And she would soon, soon be coming home. Jane danced the Lamb's letter round the table twice. And a third letter from the country: the kind lady who kept the Lamb could not keep him any longer. He was wanted at home.
New word: homeward - toward home. Some words are so good they make a whole page warm just by standing in it.

"You see," said the Psammead, watching them dance round the parlor. "The wish did not sweep the road clear before you. It turned all the little weather-vanes your way, and you walked, and here you are." The children were too happy to answer. They hugged the grumpy old Sand-fairy till its fur stood up all wrong. For once, the Psammead did not mind being hugged at all.

There was good news, too, for the learned gentleman. Great people had read his papers at last. He was invited to Egypt itself, to dig where the old temples stood. He was going to see the country he had loved all his life. He came down to tell the children, with his hat in his hands, looking ten years younger. Cyril carried his box up to him that same evening, full of the best of everything.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Psammead's Farewell
chapters.artPrompt: a small brown furry creature with long snail eyes on stalks standing on an open moonlit windowsill looking back at four children, its fur silver-edged by moonlight, the glowing amulet on the wall behind, an empty warm parlor with dying fire, deep blue night beyond the window, tender bittersweet storybook illustration

blocks.text: The night before the homecoming, the Psammead called them together in the moonlit parlor. The house was quiet, and the moon lay in a white square on the floor. Its fur was sleek, its snail eyes were bright, and it stood up very straight, like a small brown judge. "It is time," it said. "Wishes and I are old friends, but I am two thousand years old, and I want my sleep."
The Psammead says good-bye, gruff and kind, under the quiet moon.

"Must you go?" asked Jane, with tears. "Everything must, my dear, and everything does. Then everything comes round again, if you wait." The Psammead looked at each child in turn. "You were the best children I ever wished for. Not because you were clever. Because you learned to wish for each other." Jane wiped her eyes, and laughed, and wiped them again.
Talk together: The Psammead calls the children its best ever. What had they learned about wishing that made them deserve those words?

It let them kiss the top of its grumpy head, which it had never allowed before. Then it trudged to the open window and paused on the sill, with the moon behind it. And then it was gone, as sand is gone when the wind has finished. The sill was empty, and only the moonlight stayed. The Amulet, on its nail, grew cool and quiet.

"Will we ever see it again?" asked Robert. "In two thousand years," said Cyril, "someone will dig it up. And I hope it grumbles at them exactly as it grumbled at us." Outside, the garden was very still, and smelled of night flowers. They hung the Amulet carefully back on its nail, where it shone like a small, still moon. It looked, Anthea thought, like a lamp turned very low.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · All Together
chapters.artPrompt: a warm lamplit parlor where a bearded sea captain father lifts a laughing baby, a mother wrapped in furs laughing beside him, four children and an old nurse crowded round with shining faces, the joined amulet glowing faintly on the wall, teapot and fire and deep evening light, joyful tender storybook illustration

blocks.text: Then came the day they had waited a whole long year of letters for. The door banged downstairs, and feet came running up. Father stood in the parlor - brown, bearded, real, with his arms open. Behind him came Mother, well again, wrapped in furs and laughing. The Lamb rode on her shoulder, shouting "Dada!" at the top of his voice. Old Nurse's kettle was already singing upstairs, as if it had known too.
The door opens, and the family is together at last, all safe.

Old Nurse cried into her apron, and the learned gentleman shook Father's hand. The parlor was so full of noise that the teapot could hardly be heard. The Lamb grabbed Cyril's nose, which is the old way of saying you are home. The Amulet hung on its nail, quiet as a plain little charm. It had done its work. Some magic, like some love, does not need to shine once it has come true.
Question for you: The magic is over, but the happiness goes on. Which of the two do you think lasts longer - and why?

On the shelf the children kept the Amulet still, both halves joined. It was cool to the touch, and it kept its own counsel about time. Sometimes, on moonlit nights, Anthea thought it gleamed very faintly, like something remembering. And once she was almost sure she heard, far away, a small grumpy voice snoring in the sand. But the house was warmer than any shelf, and fuller than any museum.

Father told stories of the sea, Mother grew rosy in the London fog, and the Lamb grew fat and loud. The parlor lamp burned late every evening, and nobody wanted to be the first to bed. And the four children knew what they knew now: that time is long, but love is longer. Some wishes, once made well, never stop coming true.
